scoring_methodology.description: Composite score (0–100) for station priority, used to rank which stations to build first.

factors.name: car_ratio
factors.source: car_count / total — higher car % = more LRT modal shift potential

factors.name: network_centrality
factors.source: number of route connections at this node in the road network

factors.name: geographic_coverage
factors.source: spatial distribution — avoids clustering stations too close together

plans.name: Mittraphap N–S Spine
plans.description: Single north-south line along Highway 2 (Mittraphap Road) connecting KKU to southern suburbs.
plans.reasoning: Mittraphap Road (Highway 2) is the primary arterial corridor running north-south through Khon Kaen. It carries 5,000–6,700 veh/hr consistently and has the highest car ratio in the network (74% at Mittraphap North), indicating strong modal shift potential. This plan connects KKU (45,000 students/staff) directly to the city center and southern suburbs with the simplest possible infrastructure.
pros: Follows the city's primary arterial corridor with consistent 5,000–7,000 veh/hr
Highest car ratio (74% at Mittraphap North) = strong modal shift potential
Connects Khon Kaen University — a major trip generator (~45,000 students/staff)
Single-line construction = lowest cost and simplest operations
Serves the intercity bus corridor (links to NE Thailand)
cons: Zero east-west coverage; misses the densest city core streets
Only 6 stations — limited catchment area
Southern terminus (Kudkwang) is low-density; may have weak ridership
Does not serve major markets (Jomphon, Banglamphu, Nongkhotr)
No transfer opportunities to other future lines

plans.name: East–West City Core
plans.description: Single east-west line through the densest traffic zone connecting Srichan to Kasikorn corridor.
plans.reasoning: The east-west corridor through the city core contains the 3 highest-traffic measurement points in the entire dataset (8,298 + 7,426 + 7,419 veh/hr). This line passes through Central Plaza, multiple markets, hospitals, and government buildings. Short length (~5 km) means fast construction and the highest projected ridership per kilometer.
pros: Serves the 3 highest-traffic corridors (8,298 + 7,426 + 7,419 veh/hr)
Passes through multiple commercial hubs — Central Plaza, markets, hospitals
Short line ≈ 5 km = fast construction (2–3 years) and low capital cost
Highest projected ridership per kilometer of any single-line option
Connects both the western suburbs (Nongkhotr) and eastern zone (Jomphon market)
cons: No connection to KKU — the largest single trip generator in the city
No north-south mobility; Mittraphap commuters are unserved
Limited suburban reach — most stations are within the inner 3 km
Does not address the congested Kalapha corridor to the north
Ruen Rom station area has high motorcycle share (35%) with lower LRT conversion

plans.name: X-Cross Dual Lines
plans.description: Two intersecting lines (N–S + E–W) forming an X with interchange at Central Junction.
plans.reasoning: Combining Plans 1 and 2 creates a comprehensive X-shaped network that covers both the N-S Mittraphap corridor and the E-W city core. The interchange at Central Junction (62% car ratio, 7,269 veh/hr) maximizes transfer utility. KKU students can reach the eastern commercial zone via a single transfer. Can be phased: build Red Line first for the KKU connection, then add Blue Line.
pros: Comprehensive coverage in both axes — serves 80% of high-traffic corridors
Central Junction interchange maximizes transfer utility and system ridership
KKU connected to city core AND eastern commercial zones via single transfer
Balanced geographic reach — north, south, east, and west all served
Can be phased: build Red first, add Blue later to distribute cost
cons: Highest capital cost among dual-line proposals — 2 full lines (≈ 18 km total)
Complex interchange station (Central) requires expensive underground/elevated construction
12 stations to build/maintain = highest operational expenditure
Some stations (Mittraphap South, Srichan-Nongkhotr) may underperform
Construction period ≈ 5–7 years causes prolonged traffic disruption

plans.name: University Express
plans.description: Direct connection from KKU (Mo Din Daeng) to Central via the Kalapha corridor.
plans.reasoning: KKU is the single largest trip generator in Khon Kaen with ~45,000 students and staff. Mo Din Daeng station has an extraordinary 86% car ratio — meaning almost no motorcycles — which indicates the highest modal shift opportunity in the city. The Kalapha corridor has active transit-oriented development potential with new condos and mixed-use projects.
pros: Direct KKU-to-city service — serves 45,000 students/staff daily
Follows Kalapha Road which has active transit-oriented development potential
Short line (≈ 5 km) = moderate cost with high-impact ridership
Mo Din Daeng has 86% car share — maximum modal shift opportunity
Terminus at Central enables future line extensions
cons: Very narrow catchment — only serves the NW-to-center corridor
Demand heavily skewed to class hours (peaks only 6 hrs/day)
Misses the entire eastern city (Kasikorn, Klang Mueang, Ruen Rom)
Only 5 stations — insufficient to justify heavy rail investment alone
Kalapha-Sithan and Kalapha-BMW have lower traffic (3,200–3,300 veh/hr)

plans.name: Inner City Ring
plans.description: Circular loop connecting all major city-center streets — no terminal turnarounds needed.
plans.reasoning: The inner city has a rough grid of streets (Pracha Samoson to the north, Ruen Rom to the south, Srichan to the west, Chalerm Phra Kiat to the east). A ring line circling this core serves all city-center destinations without requiring terminal turnarounds. Every station is within 500m of a major commercial/civic destination. This design is common in European cities for dense urban cores.
pros: Serves the entire city core perimeter — multiple access points to CBD
Loop operation eliminates terminal turnaround; trains run continuously
Good for short inner-city trips (shopping, government offices, markets)
Every station is within 500m of a major commercial/civic destination
Moderate construction cost — compact alignment within existing road ROW
cons: No radial connections to suburbs — KKU, Mittraphap corridor, and outskirts unserved
Circular routing adds travel time vs. a direct line (you may ride 70% of loop)
Ring has no natural growth path — hard to extend to suburbs later
Complex signal management at junctions for loop service
Several stations (Lang Mueang, Chalerm Phra Kiat) have lower demand (<3,300 veh/hr)

plans.name: Outer Orbital Loop
plans.description: Large suburban ring connecting all outer nodes — designed to reduce cross-city car trips.
plans.reasoning: Many cross-city trips currently go through the congested city center because there is no orbital road. An outer ring rail connecting KKU, the military camp, Kasikorn corridor, Lao Nadi, Ban Kok, and the Kalapha corridor would intercept these trips at the periphery, reducing inner-city congestion. This is similar to London's Overground or Tokyo's Yamanote Line concept.
pros: Maximum geographic coverage — reaches all suburban zones
Connects 12 stations across the full metro area perimeter
Reduces cross-city car trips that currently overload inner roads
Catalyzes development along the orbital corridor (TOD potential)
Links KKU, military camp, Lao Nadi, and southern Mittraphap in one loop
cons: Most expensive single-line option (≈ 25 km) — very high capital cost
Many segments pass through low-density areas = low ridership/km
Full loop travel time ≈ 55 min — impractical for cross-city trips
Does not directly serve the dense city core (passengers must transfer)
Lao Nadi West (4,557 veh/hr) and Ban Kok (3,876) are marginal stations

plans.name: Maliwan–Kasikorn Diagonal
plans.description: NW-to-SE diagonal crossing through Central — connects underserved Maliwan suburbs to eastern city.
plans.reasoning: The NW suburbs (Maliwan, Sithan) are currently the most transit-underserved area despite having a 68% car ratio at Maliwan station — indicating car-dependent residents who would switch to rail. A diagonal line through Central and then SE to Kasikorn (the busiest point at 8,298 veh/hr) creates a unique corridor not duplicated by any existing road.
pros: Unique corridor not paralleled by any existing arterial road
Connects the underserved NW suburbs (Maliwan/Sithan) to the city
Passes through Central Junction — high-demand interchange node
Captures the Kasikorn corridor (8,298 veh/hr — city's busiest point)
Moderate length (≈ 8 km) — balanced cost vs. coverage
cons: Diagonal alignment doesn't match dominant N–S or E–W travel patterns
NW terminus (Maliwan) has the lowest demand in the dataset (2,793 veh/hr)
Completely misses KKU — the largest single trip generator
No connection to the Mittraphap highway corridor
Requires complex routing through narrow city-center streets

plans.name: T-Network
plans.description: Main N–S spine with an eastward branch from Central — efficient hybrid coverage.
plans.reasoning: A T-network combines the strengths of the N-S spine with the high-demand city core branch, using Central as the natural branching point. Operationally simpler than a full X-cross because trains can alternate destinations (some go south, some go east) from a single trunk. The trunk (KKU–Central) has the clearest demand justification, and the branch captures the dense core.
pros: Combines N–S backbone with E–W city core access via single branch
Efficient use of Central as junction point — natural branching location
Can be constructed in 2 phases: spine first, branch second
Covers 9 stations across both axes with less track than X-Cross
Branch captures the 3 highest-demand city-core stations
cons: Branch line creates operational complexity (splitting/joining trains)
Southwest direction is completely unserved (no Lao Nadi or Srichan-West)
Bottleneck risk at Central junction — all passengers converge here
Uneven service: branch may have lower frequency than main trunk
Still doesn't reach Srichan-Nongkhotr (7,426 veh/hr — 2nd highest point)

plans.name: Trident Hub-Spoke
plans.description: Three branches radiating from Central Junction — north to KKU, east to Kasikorn, south to suburbs.
plans.reasoning: A trident/hub-spoke design maximizes directional coverage from a single central hub. Central Junction becomes the transit heart of the city, enabling north (KKU), east (markets/commercial), and south (suburbs/intercity) access. Each branch can be built independently — allowing flexible construction phasing based on budget and political priority.
pros: 3-directional reach from a single hub — north, east, and south
Central station becomes a major transit hub (high utilization)
Each branch can be built independently — flexible phasing
Branch B captures the densest city-core traffic corridor
Branch A provides the critical KKU connection
cons: ALL transfers require Central station — single point of failure
No cross-suburb connectivity (e.g., KKU to Kasikorn requires 2 transfers at Central)
Central station overcrowding risk — 3 lines converge on one platform
Higher operational cost — 3 branches need independent service schedules
West side (Srichan-Nongkhotr, Maliwan) completely unserved

plans.name: Full Grid Network
plans.description: 3-line comprehensive system — maximum coverage with multiple interchanges for a future-proof network.
plans.reasoning: The full grid provides maximum network resilience with 3 interchange stations (Central, Mittraphap North, Mo Din Daeng). Red handles the primary N-S demand, Blue handles the dense E-W core, and Green adds the underserved NW Maliwan corridor while connecting to KKU. Multiple interchanges mean passengers aren't funneled through a single bottleneck. This is the 'ultimate plan' — expensive but future-proof for a city of 400,000+.
pros: Maximum coverage — serves virtually all 25 measurement corridors
Multiple interchange points (Central, Mittraphap N, Mo Din Daeng) = network resilience
Future-proof: accommodates city growth in all directions
3 lines reduce single-corridor overloading and distribute demand
Green Line adds the underserved NW Maliwan corridor
cons: Extremely expensive — ≈ 30 km of track, 18 stations across 3 lines
Construction period 10–15 years = very long disruption and payback
Some stations (Maliwan, Nong Phai, Lao Nadi East) may be chronically underutilized
3-line operations require a sophisticated control center and fleet
Green Line endpoints are the lowest-demand areas in the dataset
